program_overview.title: AI and Machine Learning for Teens
program_overview.tagline: Not another course about using AI. Ten months of building it: real models, trained and evaluated by a teenager who understands what is inside them.
program_overview.description:
Most teens use AI daily; almost none understand it, and understanding is where all the opportunity lives. This live online course takes students aged 13 to 18 from zero, no coding assumed, to genuinely training, evaluating and shipping machine learning models: Python and the data stack first, then real machine learning with scikit-learn, neural networks built up from a single neuron, convolutional networks that see, language models that read, and the modern generative AI layer, understood from the inside and used through teen-legal tools with parent-involved accounts.

Honesty shapes the syllabus. Fields like reinforcement learning, robotics and ML infrastructure are named and mapped, not squeezed in as fake weeks; the depth goes where a teen can actually build: vision projects with their own trained models, an NLP project on real text, a generative AI application with guardrails, and a final capstone defended at demo day. The maths is taught as needed, school algebra is enough to start, and every concept lands in code the same week it is explained.

The pace is real: ten months at two live classes a week plus three to four hours of practice, with two more months in hand when needed. Homework after every class, monthly mixed reviews that reach back deliberately, phase exams, and a final exam that decides the certificate, with focused revision and a free retest. Real models, real evaluation, depth over dopamine.
what_makes_this_different: Builders, not passengers: teens train, evaluate and ship their own models, they do not just prompt someone else’s
Maths handled honestly: taught as needed from school algebra, never assumed, never hand-waved
Evaluation is the moral core: overfitting, leakage and misleading accuracy are taught as hard as the models themselves
Generative AI from the inside: how LLMs and diffusion actually work, plus building on them through teen-legal tools with parent-involved accounts
An honest 10-month arc with 2 months of margin: the frontier fields are mapped truthfully as next steps, not faked as weeks
Real assessment: weekly homework, monthly mixed reviews, and a final exam that decides the certificate, with focused revision and a free retest

faqs.question: What AI projects will my teen actually build?
faqs.answer: Twenty-plus real builds across ten months: honest data analyses and a first evaluated classifier in phase 1, a hand-built neural network and properly trained deep models in phase 2, an image classifier trained on a dataset they collect themselves and an NLP project on real text in phase 3, and in phase 4 a generative AI application with guardrails plus the final capstone, a complete AI project shipped as a usable demo with a model card, defended at demo day.

faqs.question: How long does it take a teenager to learn AI and machine learning?
faqs.answer: To genuinely training and evaluating models: 10 months at 2 live classes a week plus 3 to 4 hours of practice, starting from zero coding. The course keeps 2 months of margin in hand for students who need more repetition, up to 12 months with no penalty. The first trained model happens in month 3; the understanding compounds from there.

faqs.question: How is my teen assessed? Is the certificate just for attending?
faqs.answer: No. Homework follows every class, each month ends with an assignment that deliberately mixes new material with earlier topics, every phase closes with an exam, and the course ends with a final exam: a practical model-building task plus written questions from the whole syllabus. Passing earns the certificate; falling short earns focused revision and a free retest. In a field this hyped, honest assessment is the product.

faqs.question: How much maths does my teen need beforehand?
faqs.answer: School algebra is enough to start. The genuinely needed maths, vectors, a working feel for gradients, probability basics, is taught exactly when a model requires it, in code and pictures before symbols. Teens consistently find the maths easier here than at school, because it finally does something visible.

faqs.question: Do we need an expensive computer or paid software?
faqs.answer: No. A normal laptop is enough: heavy training runs on free cloud notebooks with free GPU time, and the entire toolchain, Python, scikit-learn, PyTorch and the notebooks themselves, is free. Where a generative AI service needs an account, it is set up together with a parent.

faqs.question: Is this course about using AI tools like ChatGPT, or building AI?
faqs.answer: Building, with using in its proper place. The heart of the course is training and evaluating real models. The generative layer is then learned from the inside, how LLMs and diffusion models actually work, and built upon through APIs and teen-legal tools. A teen who only prompts is a passenger; this course produces drivers. For a tools-first path we run a separate AI Tools course.

faqs.question: What can my teen do after finishing?
faqs.answer: Enter our college-level AI/ML masterclass years ahead of schedule, take the Codex and Claude Code course to build with AI agents, carry the portfolio into school science fairs and university applications, or continue into data science. The frontier fields, reinforcement learning, robotics, ML infrastructure, are mapped honestly during the course as real next roads.

faqs.question: How do we try a class before enrolling?
faqs.answer: Book a free demo class with no commitment at learn.modernagecoders.com/contact or message us on WhatsApp at +91 91233 66161. Your teen will train a tiny model inside the demo itself; that moment usually decides things.

faqs.question: Are classes live with a teacher?
faqs.answer: Always: live 1-hour sessions with a real instructor in small groups, never pre-recorded videos. Machine learning is full of silent failure modes, a leaked dataset, a misread metric, and live eyes on a student’s notebook is the only honest way to catch them early.
